title: What lights a person?
hookLine: a king asks a sage what we see by when every light goes out
carry: the mind is seen; the self is the light
last: THE WORLD IS REAL; THE MIND ADDS THE COLOR.

lines: WHAT DOES A PERSON SEE BY?
AND WHEN ALL OF THEM GO OUT?
cards: King Janaka, the king who stayed free inside a palace, has a question for the sage Yajnavalkya, and it sounds almost too simple. What does a person see by? By the sun, says Yajnavalkya.
And when the sun has set? By the moon. And when the moon has set too?
By firelight. And when the fire goes out? By a voice: in the dark, you walk toward the sound.
And when the voice falls silent, Yajnavalkya, what light does a person have then? The sage answers: the self is his light.

teach.b: That conversation is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, one of the oldest.

Its word for that inner light is atman, the self, and it's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: underneath your thoughts and moods is something that isn't a thought or a mood. It's the light they're seen by.
Patanjali, in his own school's language, calls it purusha, the seer, and today's sutras argue for it.
Sutra 4.18: the turnings of the mind are always known to their master, because the seer does not change. Always. Every thought, even the ones you'd rather nobody saw.
Then 4.19: na tat svabhasam drishyatvat. It is not self-luminous, because it is seen. Like the moon, the mind only seems to shine on its own.
It's an object, like a cup or a cloud, only subtler, and things that are seen don't light themselves. Sutra 4.21 closes the door.

teach.h: THE MIND IS SEEN, SO IT ISN'T THE LIGHT.
teach.b: If one mind were lit by another mind, you'd need a third to light that one, and a fourth, forever.

teach.h: A SEER THAT ISN'T A MIND.
teach.b: The line has to stop at a seer who isn't a mind at all. The Upanishads and the Yoga Sutras describe that seer differently, and Hindu schools still debate how.
But they agree on this much: you are not only what you see in yourself. Hindu teachers often call it the witness, sakshi. So when worry fills the room at two in the morning, notice one small thing.

teach.h: THE MIND IS SEEN; THE SELF IS THE LIGHT.
teach.b: The worry is being seen. It's real, and it's lit by something that isn't worry.

how: In Yoga and Samkhya teaching, the purusha is the unchanging witness and the mind belongs to nature; Vedanta teachers speak of the atman as the witness, sakshi, and point to the Brihadaranyaka's answer to Janaka: the self is a person's light.

o: a dark shadow the mind casts over what it sees
a calm inner voice that guides the mind in prayer
self-luminous: lit from within, which the mind is not

games.q: the king, the sage and the seer — tap the pairs.
p: asks what a person sees by
answers: the self is his light
the mind is seen, not self-lit

s: in the Upanishad, the last light Yajnavalkya names is the self
sun, moon, fire, a voice, and when all of them are gone, the self is a person's light.
for Patanjali, the mind lights itself up
4.19: it is not self-luminous, because it is something seen.
if a mind could be known only by another mind, there would be no end of minds
that's the regress 4.21 points to, along with confused memory.

games.q: a thought appears and it's known. what knows it, according to 4.18?
games.why: the turnings are always known to their master, the purusha. a mind knowing a mind would need another, without end.

practice: Let the breath find its own pace, and wait for a thought to come. When it does, don't follow it; just notice, this is known, and the same with a sound, a feeling, a plan for later.
You don't have to find the knower; rest in the plain fact that each thing is seen.

wordCard.voice: Svabhasa, self-luminous — what the mind is not. It is seen, so its light is borrowed, from the purusha, the seer that does not change.

orig.note: Sanskrit svābhāsa: self-shining. sva (self) + ābhāsa (light, appearance). the mind, says 4.19, is not this.

carryVoice: Your line: the mind is seen; the self is the light. When every other light went out, that one was left. Day four hundred eighty-five, done.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.2–4.3.6 (Janaka asks what light a person has; sun, moon, fire, speech; the self is his light)
Yoga Sutras 4.18, 4.20–4.21 (always known to the purusha; not both at once; no mind known by another mind)
